d: The specific cause that precipitated a transaction's transition to the aborted_state, such as a constraint violation, deadlock detection timeout, explicit ROLLBACK request, or application-defined failure; distinct from the aborted_state itself which is the terminal condition.

The intermediate state of rows modified by a transaction that later aborted; the partial_effects_undone that existed between the first write and the rollback completion, representable as before_image/after_image pairs in the undo_log.
The terminal transaction_state after rollback completes; all acquired locks are released and the transaction cannot be restarted automatically.
aborted_state captures the abort_reason that triggered rollback: constraint_violation, deadlock_timeout, user_abort, or system_failure.
aborted_state records the partial_effects_undone: the set of modifications that were rolled back to their before-images.
aborted_state causes the recovery_log to persist an abort record enabling redo-undo recovery procedures.
aborted_state encodes the automatic_restart_forbidden property; a new transaction must be initiated explicitly.
aborted_state is the terminal transaction_state reached when rollback completes; no state transitions emanate from it.
aborted_state records the transaction_id of the transaction that entered the terminal state for recovery audit.
aborted_state signals the release of all locks acquired by the transaction under the locking_protocol; no locks persist into aborted_state.
aborted_state produces aborted_data that is invisible to committed_data consumers under the isolation_level; other transactions perceive no effect.
The four guarantees of database transactions: atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability — the foundational contract between a DBMS and its clients.
The initial transaction_state: transaction is executing, holding locks, accumulating changes in transaction_log.
An application-defined lock with no automatic database effect; the application is responsible for enforcing its meaning and usage pattern.
The state of a row resulting from a transaction's modification; stored for redo in write_ahead_logging systems to guarantee durability alongside atomicity.
The conceptual guarantee that a transaction executes as an indivisible unit: either every operation succeeds or no operation has any effect.
The Algorithm for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics: a precise recovery procedure using transaction_log, undo_log, and redo_log to achieve atomicity and durability.
The all-or-nothing property: a transaction's effects are either fully applied or fully absent; implemented via undo_log and transaction rollback.
A mode where each individual SQL statement is implicitly wrapped in its own transaction, committing immediately upon statement completion.

A protocol constraint requiring that a transaction in the aborted_state cannot be re-executed automatically by the database; the application must explicitly reissue the transaction, distinguishing abort from retryable failure.
A timestamp_ordering scheme where each data item maintains read_timestamp and write_timestamp; transactions violating these abort.
The committed database state of a row immediately before a transaction modifies it; recorded in the undo_log so the modification can be undone if the transaction rolls back.
commit point: the precise instant when a transaction transitions from active to committed; the log sequence number position where durable persistence is guaranteed
commit log record: the write-ahead log entry that atomically records the commit point; contains transaction identifier and commit LSN
commit sequence number (CSN): a monotonically incrementing identifier assigned to each committed transaction; provides total ordering of committed state changes
commit durability: the guaranteed persistence property that all writes of a committed transaction survive system crashes; realized via write-ahead log
commit visibility: the isolation property that all writes of a committed transaction become visible to subsequent read_committed queries in other transactions
commit LSN: the log sequence number position of the commit log record; the fence above which all prior transaction writes are durable
commit barrier: the synchronization point ensuring all prior transaction writes are flushed to durable storage before any subsequent transaction commits
commit acknowledgment: the confirmation signal returned to the client indicating successful durable persistence of the transaction
commit completion: the terminal state transition from active to committed; releases all locks held exclusively and schedules release of shared locks per protocol
commit promise: the contractual guarantee to the user that transaction effects are durable and will survive any subsequent system restart
commit propagation: the process by which committed transaction effects become visible in the committed_data universe accessible to read_committed queries
group commit: an optimization that batches multiple transaction commit operations into a single durable write to improve throughput
commit vote: in distributed commit protocols the yes vote from a participant indicating readiness to commit; required before coordinator records decision
commit decision: the coordinator's recorded choice (commit or abort) in two-phase commit; propagates to all participants
commit timestamp: the wall-clock time recorded when commit point is established; used for versioning and serialization in timestamp-based CC
A theorem stating that a distributed system can provide at most two of three properties: consistency, availability, and partition tolerance.
A recoverable_schedule where transactions only read data committed before the transaction began; prevents cascading aborts.
A consistency model guaranteeing that causally related operations appear in order across all nodes; weaker than strong_consistency but stronger than eventual_consistency_level.
A consistent point-in-time snapshot of the database state written to durable storage, reducing recovery time by bounding how far recovery must replay logs.
The oldest active transaction_id below which all row versions are guaranteed visible to all current transactions.
The act of making a transaction's effects permanent: flush log records to durable storage, release locks, transition transaction_state to committed.
temporal threshold in read_committed: a datum is visible iff its committing_transaction committed before the reading statement started
The terminal transaction_state after durable persistence of all changes; locks are released per locking_protocol rules.
A temporal boundary condition: only modifications committed before the statement_start are visible; uncommitted changes are invisible.
database state resulting from successfully completed transactions; constitutes the visible universe for read_committed queries
The state of a row or data item after its modifying transaction has committed, making it visible to concurrent read_committed statements.
An atomic primitive that atomically compares a memory value with an expected value and swaps it if equal; used in lock_free_cc for conflict-free updates.
An optimistic_cc pattern using compare_and_swap on a version or sequence number to detect concurrent modifications without locking.
A reverse operation executed to undo the effects of a saga step when a subsequent step fails, restoring the system to a consistent state.
The compensatory action taken to reverse a transaction's effects, encompassing rollback via undo_log as the primary compensation mechanism.

A corrective operation executed when forward undo via undo_log is impossible; used in distributed systems where original transaction steps cannot be directly reversed, preserving atomicity through logically equivalent alternatives.
The set of mechanisms a DBMS uses to manage simultaneous access to shared data while preserving correctness and isolation guarantees.
A configuration parameter (often database pool size) controlling the maximum number of concurrent transactions or connections.
The mechanism in optimistic_cc determining whether a transaction's read_set or write_set overlaps with another transaction's write_set in a forbidden way.
A schedule property where serializability can be proven by analyzing the conflict graph of read/write operations; achievable with strict_two_phase_locking.
A concurrency control mechanism restricting the number of concurrent database connections to bound resource usage and lock_contention.
A distributed algorithm enabling distributed_transaction participants to agree on a single value or decision; used alongside two_phase_commit for fault tolerance.
A variant of two_phase_locking where all locks are acquired before the transaction begins, eliminating deadlock entirely at the cost of reduced concurrency.
A transaction transforms the database from one valid state to another, preserving all defined integrity constraints and business rules.
An isolation_level specific to cursor-based reads: locks are held only on the current row, providing a middle ground between read_uncommitted and read_committed.
A failure condition where all connections in a connection_pool are consumed by blocked transactions waiting for locks, preventing new transactions from starting.
A logical unit of work executed against a database, bounded by BEGIN and COMMIT/ROLLBACK, guaranteeing ACID properties across one or more SQL operations.
A cycle of transactions each waiting to acquire a lock held by the next transaction in the cycle, causing all involved transactions to block indefinitely.
The process of identifying when a deadlock has formed, typically via a wait_for_graph analyzed by lock_manager.
The frequency with which lock_manager runs deadlock detection; shorter intervals catch deadlocks faster at higher CPU cost.
The rate at which deadlocks occur in the system; indicates whether deadlock_prevention or deadlock_detection thresholds need tuning.
Protocols that ensure deadlocks cannot occur by ordering lock acquisition or assigning priorities that determine which transaction rolls back.
An anomaly where a transaction reads data written by another transaction that has not yet committed; only possible in read_uncommitted.
An anomaly where one transaction overwrites an uncommitted value written by another transaction, violating atomicity and potentially causing inconsistency.
Lock management across multiple database nodes using a distributed lock service; required for distributed_transaction coordination.
A transaction spanning multiple database nodes or storage systems; requires coordination protocols like two_phase_commit for atomicity.
A periodic snapshot of the database state written to durable_storage that bounds recovery time by reducing the log interval that must be scanned during crash_recovery.
The committed transaction_state transition where all redo_log entries are guaranteed durable and the transaction is guaranteed to survive any subsequent crash.
The process of restarting the database and using transaction_log to reconstruct the committed_data state as of the moment of crash, ensuring no durability contract is broken.
The physical medium or storage subsystem that guarantees bitwise persistence of written data across power loss, hardware failure, and system crashes; the endpoint of all durability guarantees.
The synchronous I/O operation that transfers log buffers from volatile memory to durable_storage; must complete before commit returns success to the client.

The subsystem that enforces durability by reconstructing the committed database state from transaction_log after a crash; scans log forward to redo committed changes and backward to undo uncommitted ones.
Log records describing the after-image of modified data; during recovery the manager reapplies these records to restore committed transaction effects.
Log records describing the before-image of modified data; used during rollback and recovery to reverse uncommitted changes, preserving durability by ensuring only committed effects survive.

A protocol mandating that log records describing modifications be flushed to durable_storage before the corresponding data pages are written to disk; foundational mechanism for both atomicity and durability.
Once a transaction commits, its effects persist permanently even after system crash; guaranteed by write_ahead_logging and recovery_manager.
A consistency model where updates propagate asynchronously and all replicas converge to the same state given no new updates; relevant in distributed_transaction.
A consistency model where reads may return stale data but the system guarantees convergence after all writes propagate and settle.
A lock type granting sole read-write access to a resource; incompatible with all other lock types including shared_lock and update_lock.
A retry strategy where the delay before each transaction_retry doubles exponentially, reducing contention and thundering herd on shared resources.
A select_for_update variant that fails immediately if any requested lock cannot be acquired rather than blocking.
A select_for_update variant that skips rows already locked by other transactions, returning only rows that can be locked immediately.
A special transaction_id older than all normal transaction_ids; row versions with frozen_xid are always visible and never garbage collected.
A lock on an index interval between two consecutive index entries; used by next_key_locking to prevent phantom_read in range queries.
The process of reclaiming row versions no longer needed by any active transaction's read_view to reclaim storage.
The property that executing an operation multiple times has the same effect as executing it once; essential for safe transaction_retry in unreliable networks.
Lock management for B-tree or hash index pages to protect structural changes during concurrent index operations.
An index scan in mvcc that satisfies a query without accessing the heap by checking visibility against index-only tuples.
MySQL InnoDB's concurrency control combining gap_lock, next_key_locking, and a sophisticated lock_manager supporting all isolation levels.
A lock mode indicating intent to acquire finer-grained locks on sub-objects; used at higher levels of lock_granularity hierarchy (table, page, row).
The property that concurrently executing transactions do not interfere with each other; the degree of interference is controlled by isolation_level.
A configurable parameter defining the degree to which concurrent transactions are isolated from each other's uncommitted or intermediate effects.
The database-specific syntax and knobs for setting isolation_level (SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL in SQL, engine-specific params).
The inverse relationship between isolation_level strength and throughput: stronger isolation requires more locking or version management overhead.
The explicit performance vs correctness choices made when selecting an isolation_level; stronger guarantees reduce concurrency and throughput.
An index-based lock protecting a specific index entry; used in next_key_locking to prevent phantom_read by locking index gaps.
A strong consistency model for distributed systems where operations appear atomic and instantaneous to all observers; stronger than serializable in some respects.
A condition where transactions repeatedly restart or change state in response to other transactions without making progress, distinct from deadlock.
The act of requesting and obtaining a lock from lock_manager before performing a read or write operation on a protected resource.
A read_committed implementation variant using shared locks acquired at read time but released before transaction commit, permitting non-repeatable reads.
A diagnostic technique tracing which transactions hold and wait on locks to identify sources of lock_contention.
A table specifying which lock modes can be held simultaneously on the same object; drives lock acquisition decisions in lock_manager.
A performance condition where many transactions compete for the same locks, causing lock_wait and degrading throughput; mitigated by lock_granularity tuning.
A mechanism where lock_manager automatically upgrades many fine-grained locks to a coarser lock when lock_contention thresholds are exceeded.
Concurrency control techniques that avoid blocking through atomic operations rather than locks; compare_and_swap is the canonical primitive.
The size of the database object protected by a lock: row_lock, page_lock, table_lock — trading off concurrency against lock_manager overhead.
The subsystem responsible for tracking held locks, responding to lock requests, building the wait_for_graph, and detecting deadlocks.
The concrete implementation of lock_manager managing lock tables, queues, compatibility checks, and deadlock detection.

The deterministic act of relinquishing every lock held by a transaction upon reaching its transaction_boundary, whether through commit or abort, restoring exclusive or shared access rights to the affected rows and index entries for other transactions.
A mechanism where a transaction waiting for a lock is aborted after a configurable elapsed period, preventing indefinite waiting.
timeout mechanism in read_committed for transactions blocked waiting to acquire conflicting locks on rows
The conversion of a held shared_lock to an exclusive_lock; requires checking lock_compatibility_matrix and may block or fail if incompatible locks exist.
A state where a transaction cannot proceed because the resource it needs is locked by another transaction; resolved by lock_manager upon lock release.
The cumulative time transactions spend blocked waiting for locks; a key metric for diagnosing lock_contention and lock_manager bottlenecks.
A mechanism where a lock_wait is abandoned after a configured duration, returning an error to the application for retry or handling.
A disciplined set of rules governing when locks may be acquired and released to ensure serializability or other isolation guarantees.
A monotonically increasing identifier for log records in write_ahead_logging; used to order recovery operations and coordinate replication.
An anomaly where two transactions both read and update the same row, and one update overwrites the other's change because of write_write_conflict.
MongoDB's lock_manager using intent locks at database and collection levels, with optimistic writes and retry on lock acquisition failure.
A timestamp_ordering scheme using mvcc: readers never block writers, writers never block readers, and conflicts trigger abort.
Multi-version concurrency control: maintain multiple versions of rows so readers and writers do not block each other, each transaction sees a snapshot.
A read_committed implementation variant using multi-version concurrency control where statements read the most recent committed version of each row.
A transaction contained within another transaction, with its own commit/rollback semantics that may be independent or subordinated to the parent.
A failure mode where nodes in a distributed system cannot communicate with each other; forces a choice between availability and consistency per CAP_theorem.
A locking_protocol combining row_lock on the accessed record with gap_lock on the surrounding interval to prevent phantom_read.
the guaranteed anomaly prevention in read_committed: a transaction may never observe uncommitted changes from concurrent transactions
An anomaly where a transaction reads the same row twice and gets different values because another transaction modified and committed between reads.
the permitted anomaly in read_committed: a transaction reading the same row twice may observe different values if a concurrent transaction updates and commits that row between reads
The temporal scope during which a reading transaction may see uncommitted changes from other transactions, bounded by those transactions' commit operations.
Concurrency control strategy that permits unrestricted execution and detects conflicts only at validation_phase, aborting and retrying on conflict.
A pattern where a version integer is incremented on each row update and checked during transaction commit to detect concurrent modifications.
Oracle Database's implementation of statement-level read consistency using undo segments to reconstruct read_view at query start.
An extension of CAP_theorem: in the presence of a network_partition, one must choose between PA (consistency) and EC (availability); otherwise EL (latency) vs C.
A lock_granularity unit protecting a disk page (typically 4–16 KB); intermediate granularity used in some storage engines.

The invariant that upon rollback all modifications performed by the transaction are reversed to match the before_image recorded in each recovery_log_entry, leaving no residual trace of the transaction's intermediate state in the database.

A condition during transaction execution where an operation fails after prior operations in the same transaction have already modified state; triggers rollback to enforce atomicity's all-or-nothing guarantee.

The enforcement mechanism ensuring that if a transaction fails at any point before transaction_boundary, no tuple modifications leak into committed_data; achieved by deferring all visible effects until commit.
A transient transaction_state after the final statement executes but before log records are flushed; failure here triggers rollback.
A consensus_protocol for reaching agreement in a distributed system with faulty nodes; provides safety guarantees even under network_partition.
Concurrency control strategy that prevents conflicts by acquiring locks before accessing data, blocking if locks are unavailable.
An anomaly where a transaction re-executes a range query and gets a different set of rows due to another transaction inserting or deleting rows in that range.
A specific manifestation of phantom_read in lock-based isolation: gap_lock or predicate_locking violations allow new rows to appear between reads.

the permitted anomaly in read_committed: a transaction executing the same range query twice may observe different row sets if concurrent transactions insert or delete rows within that range and commit
PostgreSQL's implementation of snapshot_isolation via transaction_id, version_chain, and VACUUM for garbage_collection_mvcc.
A theoretical locking mechanism that locks the set of rows satisfying a predicate, rather than specific rows or gaps; prevents phantom_read in serializable.
A consensus_protocol designed to be understandable, providing leader election and log replication as an alternative to paxos_consensus.
A consistency guarantee where a client's own writes are immediately visible to subsequent reads from that same client; a common eventual_consistency_level escape hatch.
An isolation_level where each statement sees only data committed before that statement begins; prevents dirty_read but allows non_repeatable_read and phantom_read.
read_committed allows non_repeatable_read: the statement_snapshot refreshes at each statement start, so rows read early in a transaction can change.
read_committed allows phantom_read: newly inserted committed rows can appear in subsequent statement executions within the same transaction.
read_committed provides stronger guarantees than read_uncommitted: it prevents dirty_read that read_uncommitted allows.
read_committed provides weaker guarantees than repeatable_read: it permits non_repeatable_read and phantom_read that repeatable_read prevents.
read_committed prevents dirty_read: uncommitted changes from other transactions are invisible to statements.
lock management characteristic in read_committed where shared read locks are typically released immediately after each row access rather than held to transaction end
An isolation_level variant where read transactions use an mvcc snapshot but cannot write, reducing lock contention and enabling certain optimizations.
The initial phase in optimistic_cc where a transaction reads all needed data and stores read_set for later validation.
An anomaly where a transaction reads multiple rows and sees an inconsistent state because another transaction is mid-update on those rows.
The weakest isolation_level: transactions may observe uncommitted changes from other transactions, permitting dirty_read.
The metadata defining which row versions are visible to a transaction in mvcc: transaction_id boundaries and active transaction list.
A conflict where one transaction reads stale data invalidated by another transaction's uncommitted or subsequent write.
A schedule where committed transactions never read data written by aborted transactions; a minimal correctness requirement for transaction histories.

A durable record written to the transaction log capturing a single row modification, containing the transaction identifier, the affected row identifier, the before_image, and the after_image; the recovery_subsystem uses these entries to undo uncommitted changes and redo committed changes during crash recovery.
The component responsible for restoring database consistency after failure using transaction_log and ARIES_recovery.

The database component responsible for restoring consistency after a crash by scanning the transaction log, classifying each transaction as committed uncommitted or aborted, and executing undo operations for uncommitted transactions using their recovery_log_entry records.
Log records describing changes to be reapplied during recovery to bring the database forward to a consistent state after a crash.
An isolation_level ensuring that all reads within a transaction see a consistent snapshot as of transaction start; prevents non_repeatable_read but may permit phantom_read.
Application code that re-executes a transaction_retry on transient failures (deadlock, serialization_failure, lock_timeout) before propagating errors.
The act of undoing a transaction's effects using undo_log entries, returning the database to its pre-transaction state.
Lock management at the individual row granularity via row_lock entries in lock_manager's lock table; enables high concurrency but increases lock_manager overhead.
A lock_granularity unit protecting a single row; maximum concurrency but highest lock_manager overhead and risk of lock_contention.
repeatable_read employs pessimistic locking that blocks concurrent writers at read time, unlike optimistic concurrency control which detects conflicts at commit time.

The commit event in a transaction executing under repeatable_read, marking the transaction_boundary at which all held rr_read_locks undergo lock_release and the transaction's effects become durable and visible to other transactions under the same isolation level.

Database rows that have been durably persisted by a committed transaction and fall within the rr_observation_window of a concurrent repeatable_read transaction; these rows are visible because their committing transactions committed before the repeatable_read transaction started.

An isolation_level ensuring that all reads within a transaction see a consistent snapshot of the database as of transaction start; prevents non_repeatable_read by acquiring and holding read locks on accessed rows until transaction end.
When two transactions under snapshot_isolation both attempt to modify the same row the first to commit wins and the second rolls back; not applicable to lock-based repeatable_read.
An index_range_lock on the gap between index entries acquired under repeatable_read to prevent phantom_read by blocking insert operations in that range.

The isolation_level at which a transaction sees only data committed before its start, acquires a shared rr_read_lock on every row it reads, holds all such locks until transaction_boundary, and prevents non_repeatable_read through lock semantics rather than snapshot versioning.
repeatable_read uses a locking_protocol based on shared_locks on rows and optionally index_range_locks on key ranges rather than snapshot versioning.
The temporal scope from row_read acquisition of read_lock until transaction_boundary where atomicity resolves via commit or rollback, releasing all held locks.
A mechanism to prevent indefinite blocking when write_lock acquisition is stalled by read_locks held under repeatable_read; transaction rolls back if lock not acquired within threshold.
The guarantee that repeating the same row read within a transaction always returns the same before_image; achieved by holding read_lock preventing concurrent write_lock acquisition.

The interval from transaction_start to the rr_transaction_boundary during which a repeatable_read transaction observes a frozen snapshot of the database; any rows committed by other transactions after the window opens remain invisible regardless of subsequent commit events.

A read phenomenon in weaker isolation levels where a transaction re-executing a ranged query sees new rows inserted by a concurrent transaction between executions; under rr_isolation_level this is prevented by rr_gap_lock on the index ranges spanned by the query predicates.
repeatable_read permits phantom_read when gap_lock is not enforced on the index used by the query; inserts in gaps between locked rows remain possible.
A shared_lock acquired when a row is read under repeatable_read; held until transaction commits or rolls back, preventing any concurrent transaction from acquiring a write_lock on that row.

The rollback operation executed by a transaction under repeatable_read, undoing all row modifications using recovery_log_entry before_image data, releasing all held rr_read_locks via lock_release, and transitioning the rr_transaction_state to aborted.

The moment when a repeatable_read transaction terminates via commit or rollback, concluding the rr_observation_window and triggering lock_release of all rr_read_locks acquired during the transaction's active phase.
The committed_data visible to a repeatable_read transaction is frozen at transaction_start regardless of later commits by concurrent transactions.

The phase of a transaction executing under repeatable_read, following the standard transaction_state lifecycle of active, partially_committed, committed, or aborted, where each phase drives whether rr_read_locks are held or released.
read_committed releases read_locks after each statement, permitting non_repeatable_read; repeatable_read holds read_locks through transaction_end, eliminating that anomaly.
repeatable_read uses write_lock blocking while snapshot_isolation uses mvcc versioning; snapshot_isolation prevents non_repeatable_read but allows write_skew that repeatable_read prevents.

The write_ahead_logging requirement within a lock-based repeatable_read system mandating that every recovery_log_entry be flushed to durable storage before the corresponding row modification is applied, ensuring crash recovery can reconstruct all transaction effects exactly once.
A write_lock request on a row already held with a read_lock by another transaction blocks until that transaction releases its locks at commit or rollback.
A pattern for managing distributed_transaction without ACID atomicity: each step has a compensating_transaction to undo its effects on failure.
A named marker within a transaction allowing partial rollback to that point without aborting the entire transaction.
A lock held during DDL operations (ALTER TABLE, CREATE INDEX) that prevents concurrent DML or other schema changes.
A SQL clause acquiring exclusive_lock on selected rows before returning results, preventing concurrent modifications until commit or rollback.
A consistency model where all operations appear in a globally consistent order, but that order need not correspond to real time.
The strongest isolation_level: the result of executing concurrent transactions is equivalent to some serial order of those transactions; prevents all anomalies.
A history of concurrent transaction operations producing the same result as some serial ordering of those transactions.
PostgreSQL's serializable_isolation implemented as an SSI extension to snapshot_isolation, detecting and aborting serialization_failure via SSI_detect.
A transaction abort triggered when serializable detects a write_skew or other serializability violation during commit via SSI_detect.
A lock type permitting concurrent reads by multiple transactions but preventing exclusive writes; compatible with other shared_locks, incompatible with exclusive_lock.
In lock_based_read_committed, shared locks held on rows are released before transaction commit, enabling writers to acquire exclusive locks on those rows.
A point-in-time consistent view of the database state presented to a transaction; defined by read_view in mvcc systems or by isolation_level in lock-based systems.
An isolation_level using mvcc where a transaction reads from a consistent snapshot taken at transaction start; prevents lost_update but allows write_skew.
A failure condition in distributed_locking where a partition causes two nodes to believe they each hold the same lock, leading to data corruption.
Microsoft SQL Server's snapshot_isolation using row versioning, distinct from serializable_snapshot_isolation (SI) in PostgreSQL.
The Serialized Snapshot Isolation algorithm that detects dangerous structural dependencies between concurrent transactions to identify write_skew violations.
A single SQL operation within a transaction; atomicity requires that each statement either fully completes its effect or fully reverts before the next statement begins.
guarantee within read_committed that each SQL statement sees all changes committed at the moment that statement began execution
A defining property of read_committed: unlike repeatable_read where the snapshot spans the entire transaction, each statement obtains a fresh snapshot at statement_start.
The committed state of the database as observed at the moment a statement begins within a read_committed transaction; defines the visible set of rows.
The point in time when a SQL statement begins execution in a read_committed transaction, establishing which committed changes are visible.
logical moment recorded when each statement begins, establishing the visibility cutoff point for read_committed row versions
A schedule where reads and writes of a data item occur in the same order as in a serial schedule; required for strict_two_phase_locking and ARIES recovery.
A variant of two_phase_locking where exclusive_locks are held until transaction end, ensuring strict_schedule and enabling cascading_less schedules.
A consistency model where all reads see the most recent committed write; requires coordination and prevents all anomalies at the cost of latency.
strict_two_phase_locking where all locks (shared and exclusive) are held until transaction end, the most common production locking_protocol.
A compact transaction identifier used in row version headers to record which transaction created or deleted a tuple.
A lock_granularity unit protecting an entire table; high lock_manager efficiency but low concurrency for partitioned or sparse tables.
An optimization of basic_timestamp_protocol that allows certain writes to be skipped rather than aborted, improving throughput.
An extension of two_phase_commit that adds a pre-commit phase to avoid blocking when the coordinator fails during the commit phase.
A concurrency control method assigning timestamps to transactions and using them to order operations, ensuring serializability without locking.
A log_record written when a transaction enters the aborted_state; signals that undo_log entries must be applied to reverse this transaction's effects.
A log_record written when a transaction transitions to the active transaction_state; records transaction_id and start timestamp but no data modifications.
A special log_record written periodically by a checkpoint_writer; records the volatile database state at a consistent point, bounding the recovery_manager's replay horizon.
The subsystem component that periodically writes a tl_checkpoint_record to the transaction_log; trims obsolete log segments and bounds crash_recovery time.
A log_record written when a transaction commits; marks the durable persistence boundary for durability guarantees; flushed to disk before the transaction releases its locks.
A runtime data structure maintained by recovery_manager listing data pages modified but not yet flushed; consulted during checkpoint to ensure write_ahead_logging invariants hold.
The act of transferring the contents of tl_log_buffer to durable storage; triggered by transaction commit, tl_log_buffer overflow, or a periodic checkpoint; O(1) or O(n) bounded by buffer size.

A volatile in-memory page or ring buffer where tl_log_record entries are assembled before flush; resides in the transaction's write_ahead_logging envelope and is flushed as a whole to durable storage.
The fundamental unit of a transaction_log: a single append-only entry recording one atomic change or lifecycle event made by a transaction; identified by an lsn.
Log Sequence Number: a monotonically increasing numeric identifier assigned to each tl_log_record; enables total ordering, O(1) record retrieval, and dependency tracking between log entries.

The subsystem that, on system restart, reads the transaction_log from the last tl_checkpoint_record forward; replays committed tl_redo_log entries and rolls back uncommitted transactions using tl_undo_log.
A log_record or series of tl_update_record entries capturing the after_image of modifications; replayed by recovery_manager to idempotently reconstruct committed changes after a crash.
A structured collection of tl_update_record entries chained by a transaction; traversed in reverse order during rollback to restore the before_image of each modified entity.
A log_record capturing a before_image and after_image of a modified data page or row; used by both redo_recovery (for durability) and undo_recovery (for atomicity rollback).

Write-Ahead Logging: the protocol requiring that a tl_log_record be flushed to durable storage before the corresponding data modification is written to the database page; the primary mechanism for durability.

The demarcation point between consecutive transaction executions defining the scope over which atomicity applies; all effects within are committed or none are, with no partial visibility across the boundary.
A monotonically increasing identifier assigned to each transaction; the basis for snapshot_isolation read_view construction and visibility_check.
An append-only sequence of records tracking every change made by transactions; the primary mechanism for atomicity and durability.
The component coordinating transaction boundaries, lock acquisition, commit, and rollback across database operations.
The act of a transaction executing a read operation; at read_uncommitted this read may return uncommitted_change from concurrent transactions.
The process of re-executing a transaction that aborted due to conflict_detection or serialization_failure; may use exponential_backoff.

The consistent view of the database state constructed at a transaction's start point, containing all rows whose committing transactions committed before that moment and excluding uncommitted rows and rows from later commits; the snapshot provides the read-consistent foundation for isolation guarantees.
The current phase of a transaction lifecycle: active, partially_committed, committed, aborted; drives lock release and recovery behavior.
A database internal table tracking the status of all in-flight transactions for visibility_check and recovery purposes.
The number of transactions per unit time a database can process; directly impacted by lock_contention, lock_granularity, and isolation_level.
A distributed_transaction commit protocol with a prepare phase followed by a commit phase, ensuring atomicity across all participants.
The two-phase commit protocol coordinating commit of a distributed_transaction across participant nodes: coordinator asks prepare then commit/abort.
A locking_protocol where transactions must acquire all locks during a growing_phase and release all locks during a shrinking_phase, guaranteeing conflict_serializable schedules.
A modification to database state made by a transaction that has not yet committed; visible to other transactions at read_uncommitted.
The state of a row or data item modified by an active uncommitted transaction, invisible to read_committed statements.
Log records describing the previous state of modified data; used to undo uncommitted transaction changes during rollback and recovery.
A lock acquired automatically when inserting a unique key value; prevents duplicate key violations from concurrent inserts.
A lock type that prevents deadlock during lock_upgrade: compatible with shared_lock but not with other update_locks or exclusive_locks.
PostgreSQL's garbage_collection_mvcc implementation: reclaiming dead tuple versions, freezing old transaction_ids, updating FSM.
The phase in optimistic_cc where the committing transaction verifies it has no conflicts with concurrent transactions before making changes visible.
In mvcc_read_committed, the version of a row visible to a statement is determined by the most recent committed version as of statement_start.
A linked list of row versions ordered by transaction_id, enabling a transaction to retrieve the appropriate version from read_view.
A per-object structure in optimistic_cc tracking which transactions have modified an object, used for conflict detection.
A schedule property requiring equivalence to a serial schedule on the same read and write operations; a superset of conflict_serializable, NP-hard to verify.
The algorithm determining whether a specific row version is visible to a transaction given its transaction_id and the set of active transactions.
A deadlock_prevention scheme for wounds_die: an older transaction waits for locks; a younger transaction aborts if it would need to wait (non-preemptive).
A deadlock_prevention scheme: an older transaction wounds (aborts) a younger transaction holding a needed lock; the younger waits if older.
A protocol requiring log records be flushed to durable storage before the corresponding data changes are applied; ensures durability and atomicity.
exclusive lock discipline in read_committed requiring a transaction to hold write locks on modified rows until transaction commit or rollback
The characteristic of read_uncommitted where a writing transaction does not hold an exclusive lock preventing other transactions from reading its uncommitted state.
The phase in optimistic_cc where a transaction constructs private write_set before validation against other transactions' read_sets and write_sets.
An anomaly in snapshot_isolation where two concurrent transactions each read overlapping data, modify disjoint subsets, and both commit successfully despite conflicting.
The set of modifications made by a transaction in mvcc, only visible to other transactions after the transaction commits.
A conflict between two transactions attempting to modify the same data item; prevented by exclusive_lock or last_writer-wins in mvcc.
